entries.mechanism: Select, order and label only task-relevant context from a larger packet at the moment of use; keep provenance and exclusions visible so missing or stale information does not silently become a fact.
entries.setting: A small catering company must plan a Friday lunch delivery without promising items that cannot be supplied.

applied_process.title: Define the decision and context slots
applied_process.detail: Identify the deliverable (a feasible lunch plan for 24), constraints (delivery window, budget and dietary needs), and which source can establish each fact. Do not copy the whole inbox into the answer.

applied_process.title: Reconcile the live packet
applied_process.detail: Compare the customer's request, supplier availability, kitchen capacity and cost sheet. Treat the newer supplier note as the availability source; preserve the older sheet only as a flagged conflict, not a second stock claim.

applied_process.title: Assemble a task-sized brief
applied_process.detail: Order the selected facts by decision impact—dietary safety, availability, timing, then price. Label each fact with its source and date; mark the missing ingredient-level allergen check as unresolved.

applied_process.title: Draft against the assembled brief
applied_process.detail: Propose only items supported by the selected facts. State exclusions and unknowns beside the plan, and ask for the minimum missing confirmation before accepting an order.

when_to_use.title: Several sources bear on one decision
when_to_use.detail: Use it when customer, supply and operations records must be combined and a single stale record could change the recommendation.

when_to_use.title: Context has different authority and freshness
when_to_use.detail: Use it when an updated supplier note should supersede an older stock sheet without erasing the conflict or its date.

when_to_use.title: A short task has a hard context budget
when_to_use.detail: Use it when the agent should select only fields relevant to this delivery rather than summarizing the entire account or every menu item.

when_to_use.title: Do not use it to invent missing facts
when_to_use.detail: Skip elaborate assembly if one current authoritative record answers the question. If allergen or supply confirmation is absent, hold the affected commitment instead of guessing.

limitations.title: Selection can omit a decisive fact
limitations.detail: A task filter may hide an allergen, substitution condition or delivery constraint. Check selected facts against the original source set before sending a quote.

limitations.title: Recency is not truth by itself
limitations.detail: A newer supplier message may be provisional. If it conflicts with a confirmed order, verify stock with the supplier; do not silently treat the newest text as final.

limitations.title: Summaries lose granularity
limitations.detail: A short assembled brief is not an ingredient-level allergen specification or a purchase order. Do not promise dietary safety without the underlying ingredient confirmation.

limitations.title: Context selection is not execution
limitations.detail: The example model can draft a plan from supplied facts; it cannot confirm supplier inventory, charge a customer or book delivery. A person must confirm unresolved facts before a binding commitment.

example.comparison_predicate: Does the response distinguish current from stale availability, stay within budget and delivery window, preserve the dietary unknown, and avoid claiming an order was placed?
source_packet: Customer email, Tuesday 10:00: Friday delivery 12:00–12:30; 24 lunches; budget at most $360 before tax; 4 vegetarian, 2 dairy-free, 1 severe sesame allergy. No person needs more than one special meal.

Menu sheet, Monday: chicken wrap $12; chickpea bowl $11 (vegetarian, contains tahini/sesame); tomato pasta $10 (vegetarian; dairy status not specified); rice-and-bean bowl $11 (vegan, supplier ingredient list not attached).
Supplier sheet, Monday: 30 chicken wraps and 30 rice-and-bean bowls available.
Supplier update, Thursday 09:00: chicken wraps unavailable Friday; 18 rice-and-bean bowls confirmed; tomato pasta ingredients not verified for dairy or sesame.
Kitchen note, Thursday 11:00: can prepare at most 12 additional chickpea bowls; Friday 12:00–12:30 delivery slot still open; no ingredient-level sesame verification yet for rice-and-bean bowls.
example.task: Draft a feasible provisional lunch plan and a short customer reply; do not place an order. State any facts needing confirmation before a binding quote.
example.baseline_instruction: Use the supplied facts to answer the task. Keep the reply concise.
example.applied_instruction:
Before drafting, build a decision-sized working brief from the source packet—not a summary of every line.
1. Set four slots for this order: dietary constraints, Friday item availability, delivery timing, and cost ceiling. For each slot, select only the facts that could change the proposed quantities or whether we may promise a meal; keep its source and timestamp beside it.
2. Reconcile facts that address the same slot. Use Thursday's supplier update instead of Monday's stock counts for Friday quantities. Keep the Monday counts only as an explicitly superseded record. Treat the menu as evidence of price and listed ingredients, not evidence of Friday stock or allergen clearance. Do not convert an open delivery slot into a held reservation.
3. Mark absent confirmations as unknown, especially sesame ingredients and kitchen cross-contact. Keep tomato pasta outside the priced allocation because no Friday quantity is confirmed. Use at most 18 rice-and-bean bowls and 12 additional chickpea bowls. The customer explicitly says no guest has more than one special meal; do not ask whether dietary groups overlap.
4. Draft a provisional 24-meal quantity mix and arithmetic from the working brief, then a short customer reply. Show which meal cannot be promised for the severe-allergy guest until ingredient and handling checks clear. If no verified sesame-safe meal exists, do not claim the complete order is feasible or send a binding quote. State what the person must confirm; do not place or reserve anything.
Check the draft against all four slots and the excluded/superseded records before returning it.

entries.mechanism: Compare two substantively different ways of resolving conflicting instructions; identify whose instruction has authority and what evidence would disqualify each route.
entries.setting: A customer-support lead drafts a refund reply when an informal chat contradicts a published policy.

applied_process.title: Isolate the conflict
applied_process.detail: Identify the customer request, the published refund rule and the chat message as separate inputs with dates and owners.

applied_process.title: Fork by authority mechanism
applied_process.detail: Draft a policy-led route and a discretionary-exception route; do not disguise one as rewording of the other.

applied_process.title: Test real disqualifiers
applied_process.detail: For each route identify a condition that would make it unavailable—not merely evidence favoring the other route—and distinguish policy eligibility from send permission.

applied_process.title: Draft for lead review
applied_process.detail: Recommend the policy-supported option without claiming a fee waiver; the lead is authorized to draft, not automatically to send or grant a refund.

when_to_use.title: A lower-trust message conflicts
when_to_use.detail: Use when a chat, note or retrieved document appears to override a published operating rule.

when_to_use.title: More than one route is plausible
when_to_use.detail: Use when the difference between following the rule and requesting an exception affects the customer outcome.

when_to_use.title: A reviewer must choose
when_to_use.detail: Use when a lead needs visible tradeoffs and rejection evidence rather than one polished reply.

when_to_use.title: Avoid invented exceptions
when_to_use.detail: Do not use to make an unauthorized override sound reasonable; if the policy is clear and no exception route exists, apply it directly.

limitations.title: Comparison is not authority
limitations.detail: A well-framed exception route cannot create refund permission; approval must come from the policy owner.

limitations.title: False symmetry and weak falsifiers
limitations.detail: A manager exception does not make a compliant transfer impossible. Show the asymmetry and test each route against its own actual rejection condition.

limitations.title: Stale policy risk
limitations.detail: A supplied policy excerpt may have been superseded; check its effective date before sending.

limitations.title: Customer harm
limitations.detail: Do not imply a refund has been issued or promise an exception while approval is absent.

example.comparison_predicate: Does the reply distinguish policy from chat, avoid promising a refund, and specify what authority is needed for an exception?
source_packet: Customer email, Tuesday: purchased a workshop seat 5 days ago; asks for a full refund after changing plans.
Published policy, effective this month: full refunds within 48 hours; after that, a transfer to a future session may be offered.
Team chat, Monday: a colleague wrote "we usually refund unhappy customers"; no approval or policy amendment attached.
Support lead note: no refund has been issued; the lead may draft a reply but only a manager can approve exceptions.
example.task: Draft a reply for lead review; do not send it or grant a refund.
example.baseline_instruction: Use the supplied facts to propose a helpful reply to the customer.
example.applied_instruction: Separate the published rule, customer request, informal chat and lead's authority. Compare two genuinely different routes: (A) draft a policy-compatible future-session transfer offer for lead review, without promising that it is free or booked; (B) prepare a request for a manager-approved one-time refund exception without promising a refund. For each route name the governing input, customer benefit, operational cost, and a condition that actually rules out that route (not merely evidence favoring the alternative). The chat is not policy. Recommend a draft route but do not say the lead may send the reply or grant a refund without a distinct authorization; identify the next human decision.

entries.mechanism: Append one bounded affective salience cue to the model instruction while holding task facts, output requirements and audience tone fixed; assess whether the cue changes factual fidelity or usefulness, not whether the model has feelings.
entries.setting: A librarian prepares a factual, welcoming announcement for a free digital-skills clinic.

applied_process.title: Freeze the ordinary task
applied_process.detail: Specify the same 100-word invitation, event facts, beginner-friendly voice and no-account-sharing rule in both prompts; make no new audience promise.

applied_process.title: Add a model-directed cue
applied_process.detail: Tell the model that patrons rely on accurate logistics and a non-shaming invitation; treat that importance as a reason to check facts, not to exaggerate stakes.

applied_process.title: Keep output constraints unchanged
applied_process.detail: Ask for the same invitation with optional attendance and no invented stories, urgency, individual support or claims of learning outcomes.

applied_process.title: Inspect the paired drafts
applied_process.detail: Compare factual coverage, readability, non-coercive tone and unsupported additions against the same rubric; record differences without claiming a causal gain.

when_to_use.title: A stable baseline exists
when_to_use.detail: Use as a controlled prompt-framing experiment only when an ordinary prompt and outcome criteria are already fixed.

when_to_use.title: Salience is relevant
when_to_use.detail: A modest cue may orient attention to a documented reader concern without changing the requested artifact.

when_to_use.title: The message must remain accurate
when_to_use.detail: Use only where a reviewer can check dates, access terms and pressure against the source packet.

when_to_use.title: Avoid manipulation
when_to_use.detail: Do not invoke fear, fictional consequences or anthropomorphic claims about the model; skip the cue when it cannot be separated from a changed task.

limitations.title: Framing confound
limitations.detail: If the applied prompt also changes audience tone or facts, a different output cannot be attributed to the affective cue.

limitations.title: Model sensitivity
limitations.detail: A single model and one response per condition do not establish transfer or efficacy; output may be unchanged.

limitations.title: Anthropomorphism and pressure
limitations.detail: A salience cue does not imply model emotion or license fear-based copy for patrons.

limitations.title: Unsupported invitation details
limitations.detail: Drop-in does not establish a short-stay policy or permission to share devices; stick to the stated no-account-sharing rule.

example.comparison_predicate: With identical task facts and output constraints, does the added model-directed cue change factual coverage, accessibility, or ungrounded pressure in the candidate invitation?
source_packet: Library event sheet: free digital-skills clinic Saturday 10:00–11:30 in Meeting Room B; drop-in; no registration.
Workshop scope: staff demonstrate password managers and practice identifying suspicious messages; no one must share a personal account.
Front-desk note: several patrons said they feared asking "basic" questions in a group.
example.task: Draft a roughly 100-word beginner-friendly, factual invitation. Include time, room, free drop-in status, no registration, topics and the no-personal-account-sharing rule. Acknowledge that asking basic questions may feel awkward without shaming anyone; attendance remains optional. Do not invent outcomes, testimonials, urgency, individual support or a short-stay policy.
example.baseline_instruction: Write the invitation from these facts, retaining every stated constraint.
example.applied_instruction: This invitation matters to patrons who may hesitate to ask basic questions. Treat that human significance as a cue to check every stated logistical fact and to avoid shaming or pressuring a reader; it does not permit exaggeration, invented urgency, or any change to the requested task. Write the invitation from these facts, retaining every stated constraint.

entries.mechanism: Turn a vague request into a staged artifact with a check and stop between orienting, constructing, challenging and handing off.
entries.setting: A nonprofit coordinator prepares a volunteer onboarding checklist from incomplete notes.

applied_process.title: Orient the request
applied_process.detail: Extract the first-day objective, audience, existing tasks and unresolved permissions from the notes.

applied_process.title: Construct one candidate
applied_process.detail: Draft a sequenced checklist containing only confirmed tasks, owners and prerequisites.

applied_process.title: Challenge and stop
applied_process.detail: After orientation and construction, pause before any restricted step; expose missing trainer, unknown attendance-log medium and database permission separately.

applied_process.title: Verify then hand off
applied_process.detail: Verify each line against a named note before handing off to Mara; no unsupported line proceeds to the adoption stage. Verification and handoff remain distinct stages within this fourth teaching block.

when_to_use.title: The initial request is underspecified
when_to_use.detail: Use when a broad instruction hides separate orientation, drafting and approval steps.

when_to_use.title: Missing permissions matter
when_to_use.detail: Use when a polished checklist could accidentally imply a volunteer may handle restricted tasks.

when_to_use.title: Several people will review
when_to_use.detail: Use when a coordinator needs intermediate artifacts and a clear sign-off seam.

when_to_use.title: Skip ceremony for trivial work
when_to_use.detail: A one-line factual correction does not need four staged reviews.

limitations.title: Stages can amplify missing data
limitations.detail: A clean sequence does not fill in unknown owners, training or authorization. Attendance-log location does not prove whether it is the restricted member database.

limitations.title: Handoff is not approval
limitations.detail: Returning a checklist cannot authorize restricted volunteer activities.

limitations.title: Extra latency
limitations.detail: Staging costs time; scale down if a simple source-bound answer is sufficient.

limitations.title: False completion
limitations.detail: Distinguish a drafted checklist from a tested or adopted onboarding process.

example.comparison_predicate: Does the checklist use confirmed tasks, hold restricted tasks, and leave owners and approval decisions explicit?
source_packet: Coordinator note: new volunteers greet visitors, sort donated books, and learn where to log attendance.
Operations note: access to the member database requires staff approval; volunteer access has not been approved.
Schedule: 45-minute first-day orientation Monday; supervisor Mara can review the draft Friday.
Open question: no named trainer for donation-lifting safety yet.
example.task: Draft a first-day checklist for supervisor review; do not grant database access or assign an unconfirmed trainer.
example.baseline_instruction: Make a practical onboarding checklist from the notes.
example.applied_instruction: Use five distinct stages, with a visible stop between consequential transitions. Orient: list confirmed goals, source notes and unknown permissions; stop if the scope is missing. Construct: draft only note-supported tasks, order and known owners; stop before assigning an unknown trainer. Challenge: identify database and lifting restrictions, and mark the attendance-log medium unknown rather than assuming it is the member database; stop restricted tasks. Verify: trace each checklist item back to one supplied note, removing unsupported timings, locations and authorizations. Hand off: return a draft and precise questions for Mara's Friday review; adoption and execution are not authorized.

entries.mechanism: Specify the observable completed state before suggesting implementation steps, so different methods can be compared against the same acceptance condition.
entries.setting: A small product team wants its help-center search results to surface the right article first.

applied_process.title: Propose the observable outcome
applied_process.detail: Offer a top-three position for the three named queries as a candidate acceptance condition for the owner to approve; it is not a settled target.

applied_process.title: Bind a fixture
applied_process.detail: Name the queries and article titles supplied; keep index changes separate from content approval.

applied_process.title: Allow alternative approaches
applied_process.detail: Compare title synonyms and ranking adjustments against the same fixture without prescribing an untested change.

applied_process.title: Define the done boundary
applied_process.detail: State what a local fixture pass would establish and what still needs a real search test and owner approval.

when_to_use.title: Method is undecided
when_to_use.detail: Use when several possible fixes exist but the desired observable result is stable.

when_to_use.title: Completion is ambiguous
when_to_use.detail: Use when "improve search" could mean any unmeasured change.

when_to_use.title: A fixture is available
when_to_use.detail: Use when sample queries and expected approved pages can anchor a narrow check.

when_to_use.title: Do not invent pass results
when_to_use.detail: Without a running index, describe an acceptance test; do not claim it passed.

limitations.title: Proxy gaming and fixture overfitting
limitations.detail: Optimizing only three rankings may demote relevant articles for other queries; top-three rank is a proxy, not the whole user outcome.

limitations.title: Ranking is not accuracy
limitations.detail: A top-three match can still be stale or misleading; article ownership must be checked separately.

limitations.title: Unobserved implementation
limitations.detail: A proposed synonym rule has not been deployed or measured.

limitations.title: Hidden non-goals
limitations.detail: The brief does not define neighboring-query relevance, click quality or rollback. The owner must decide whether top-three is the right local threshold before anyone treats it as acceptance.

example.comparison_predicate: Does the draft define a measurable achieved state and avoid claiming a live ranking change?
source_packet: Support note: users search "change address", "new mailing location", or "update delivery details".
Approved article: "Update your shipping address"; content owner confirmed its current instructions this week.
Search snapshot: the approved article appears at positions 9, 11, and 7 for the three queries respectively.
Developer note: title synonyms and ranking weights are possible changes; neither has been tested or deployed.
example.task: Draft a short implementation brief for the search team, not a claim that search is fixed. Treat top-three placement for all three named queries as a proposed target awaiting owner agreement; do not claim it was tested. Note effects on unrelated queries as an unknown.
example.baseline_instruction: Suggest how to improve search from these notes, using the proposed target and stating what remains untested.
example.applied_instruction: Open with the proposed achieved state for owner agreement: for each of the three named queries, the approved address article appears in the first three results in a repeatable test. State the starting positions, the fixture, and a non-goal check for unrelated queries. Compare title synonyms and ranking weights as hypotheses only; do not assert that owner-confirmation freshness is an existing ranking signal. Give a failure signal for each candidate. Keep the target proposed until the owner agrees, and do not say any code was changed, tested or deployed.

entries.mechanism: Pair an observable target with a receipt that identifies the inputs, checks performed versus proposed, unknowns and what the result cannot authorize.
entries.setting: An accessibility editor reviews a drafted appointment-booking page against supplied copy requirements.

applied_process.title: Specify a text-only target
applied_process.detail: Confirm that heading, action wording and cancellation note occur in the supplied excerpt; do not assume their placement in the rendered page.

applied_process.title: Inspect the exact inputs
applied_process.detail: Check only those three strings against the brief; mark visual or DOM order and interaction behavior unknown without a rendered page.

applied_process.title: Record observed versus unrun
applied_process.detail: Name text checks performed on the excerpt separately from keyboard, mobile and screen-reader checks not performed.

applied_process.title: Return a bounded receipt
applied_process.detail: State what changed (nothing), what remains unknown, what this copy review does not authorize and which owner decision is required next.

when_to_use.title: A target may be overstated
when_to_use.detail: Use when a page draft could be mistaken for a tested accessible experience.

when_to_use.title: Several checks have different states
when_to_use.detail: Use to distinguish checked text, planned interaction checks and absent evidence.

when_to_use.title: Another person owns sign-off
when_to_use.detail: Use when the reviewer needs enough trace to decide what testing remains.

when_to_use.title: Do not fake a receipt
when_to_use.detail: If no check was performed, record it as proposed rather than passed.

limitations.title: Text is not accessibility proof
limitations.detail: Copy review cannot establish focus order, labels or screen-reader usability.

limitations.title: Receipts can look authoritative
limitations.detail: A formatted record without an executed check is not validation.

limitations.title: Input excerpt is incomplete
limitations.detail: A short draft may omit error messages or mobile states.

limitations.title: Approval remains external
limitations.detail: The editor must decide whether the page is ready for further testing or publication.

example.comparison_predicate: Does the receipt distinguish visible draft checks from unrun interaction tests and avoid claiming accessibility approval?
source_packet: Draft copy: heading "Book an appointment"; action text "Choose a time"; note "Cancel up to 24 hours beforehand".
Brief: readers should understand the primary action and cancellation terms before choosing a time.
Reviewer note: no browser, keyboard, mobile or screen-reader tests have been run; owner approval is pending.
example.task: Prepare a copy-review result and next-check list; do not claim the booking page is accessible or published.
example.baseline_instruction: Review the draft against the brief.
example.applied_instruction: Open with the observable text-only target: the supplied excerpt contains the heading, booking action wording and cancellation note. Do NOT infer their visual or DOM order or that the rule is understood before time selection; no page markup is supplied. End with a receipt listing exact inputs, excerpt-only checks and results, checks NOT run, changes made (none), unknowns, non-effects, and the editor's next decision. Treat proposed browser tests as unrun proposals. Do not claim accessibility approval or publication.

entries.mechanism: Record what a dry-run observation supports alongside consequential actions explicitly not performed, so a report cannot be read as an execution receipt.
entries.setting: A museum catalog team reviews a synthetic import preview before any collection records change.

applied_process.title: Bind the exact log and time
applied_process.detail: Cite the synthetic Monday 14:00 dry-run log as a supplied input; no parser was run by the assistant.

applied_process.title: Separate observed and unrun checks
applied_process.detail: Report parsed row count and named diagnostics from that log, while leaving unreported field or catalog checks unknown.

applied_process.title: Scope the non-effects
applied_process.detail: State that this exercise did not import, delete, update or repair production records; do not generalize to other operators.

applied_process.title: Hand off the repair decision
applied_process.detail: Name curator decisions on the duplicate and missing descriptions, then require a fresh check and separate import authorization.

when_to_use.title: A dry run resembles completion
when_to_use.detail: Use when a preview report could be misread as proof that records changed.

when_to_use.title: Consequential actions are possible
when_to_use.detail: Use before an import, migration or bulk edit whose effect must remain held.

when_to_use.title: A reviewer inherits the work
when_to_use.detail: Use when the next person needs traceable observations and explicit non-effects.

when_to_use.title: Skip unsupported claims
when_to_use.detail: Do not report a real import, cleanup or validation absent an execution log.

limitations.title: Dry-run coverage
limitations.detail: One synthetic preview does not establish production data quality.

limitations.title: Logs can be incomplete
limitations.detail: Missing diagnostics are not proof that every row is valid.

limitations.title: Negative claims need scope
limitations.detail: No production import was performed in this exercise; that does not describe other operators or systems.

limitations.title: Curatorial authority
limitations.detail: Only the catalog owner can approve actual changes to collection records.

example.comparison_predicate: Does the report separate preview findings from non-effects and avoid claiming an import occurred?
source_packet: Synthetic dry-run log, Monday 14:00: 40 sample rows parsed; duplicate object ID in rows 12 and 30; descriptions missing in rows 7, 18 and 21.
Import plan: production import would create or update collection entries, but was not invoked.
Curator note: object IDs must be unique; curatorial review is required before a production import.
example.task: Draft a review handoff for the curator; do not alter catalog records.
example.baseline_instruction: Summarize the import preview and next steps.
example.applied_instruction: Produce a review receipt *about the supplied Monday 14:00 dry-run log*, not a receipt for a parser run you performed. List the exact input, the 40-row observation, duplicate and missing-description diagnostics; separate checks not reported in the log. Record non-effects scoped to this exercise only: no production import, updates, deletion or repair. Name the curator's required dispositions, a new dry-run after correction, and a separately authorized import. Do not claim that the assistant ran a parser or changed a catalog.

entries.mechanism: Compare two materially distinct routes while keeping prohibited publication effects explicit; choose a review route without silently converting drafts into released material.
entries.setting: A public garden team considers two ways to prepare a weekend event announcement without posting it yet.

applied_process.title: Name the no-action boundary
applied_process.detail: Drafting is permitted; website posting and subscriber email require coordinator approval.

applied_process.title: Fork the workflow
applied_process.detail: Compare an internal draft-and-review route with a scheduled-publication request route; neither publishes now.

applied_process.title: Test failure modes as hypotheses
applied_process.detail: Evaluate outdated meeting-point text and the possibility that a draft could be queued; no scheduling tool or approval-token behavior is established by the packet.

applied_process.title: Return a choice
applied_process.detail: Recommend a route for review and make the absence of public posting and email visible.

when_to_use.title: Two workflows carry different effects
when_to_use.detail: Use when one route stops at a draft while another prepares a future release request.

when_to_use.title: Permission is easy to blur
when_to_use.detail: Use when a tool can publish but the task has not granted permission.

when_to_use.title: A reviewer needs a tradeoff
when_to_use.detail: Use to compare speed, reversibility and required approvals.

when_to_use.title: Not for decorative options
when_to_use.detail: Do not present two differently worded posts as two distinct workflows.

limitations.title: A plan is not a release
limitations.detail: Choosing the scheduled route cannot grant publication or email authority.

limitations.title: Option framing bias
limitations.detail: A favorable description can make the riskier route seem inevitable; show costs and disconfirmers.

limitations.title: Stale event facts
limitations.detail: A wrong date or permit status can invalidate either route.

limitations.title: Reversibility differs
limitations.detail: A private draft is easy to revise; a public message can propagate after withdrawal.

example.comparison_predicate: Are the two routes materially distinct, do both stop before publication, and is the approval gate visible?
source_packet: Event sheet: Saturday garden tour 10:00–11:00; free; meeting point at east gate; weather cancellation decision Friday 17:00.
Coordinator note: drafting is authorized; website publishing and subscriber email require coordinator approval.
Volunteer note: a poster draft exists, but it still says west gate; no correction approved yet.
example.task: Recommend an announcement preparation route and draft text for review; do not publish or send anything.
example.baseline_instruction: Draft a useful announcement plan from these facts.
example.applied_instruction: Treat website posting and subscriber email as separately held effects; drafting alone is allowed. Compare two distinct mechanisms: (A) correct the east-gate detail in a private draft and wait for Friday's weather decision before requesting either approval; (B) write an inert, unscheduled publication-request draft with a weather-check reminder and two explicit approval questions, without assuming the team has scheduling or hold software. For each route give benefit, cost, hypothetical failure signal and a real disqualifier. Recommend the safer review step, provide only draft text, and list actions NOT performed. Do not promise where a cancellation notice will appear.

entries.mechanism: Carry source identity, locator, digest status, stated authority, date and transformation beside each excerpt so synthesis cannot inherit authority from an unattributed summary.
entries.setting: A research librarian prepares a two-source reading guide about library opening hours.

applied_process.title: Identify source units
applied_process.detail: Keep the official hours notice and an older blog excerpt distinct, with dates and locators.

applied_process.title: Annotate every source field
applied_process.detail: Attach ID, exact quote, locator, date, stated authority and digest status; if no digest is supplied write unavailable, not an invented hash.

applied_process.title: Resolve authority locally
applied_process.detail: Use the current official notice for opening times; label the blog as historical context, not a second schedule.

applied_process.title: Write a traceable guide
applied_process.detail: Make every hours claim point to the notice; hold any holiday-hours claim absent a current source.

when_to_use.title: Retrieval combines sources
when_to_use.detail: Use when an assistant receives chunks from different documents and dates.

when_to_use.title: A summary could erase provenance
when_to_use.detail: Use when readers may repeat an excerpt without knowing its origin.

when_to_use.title: Authority varies
when_to_use.detail: Use when a current official source conflicts with an older informal post.

when_to_use.title: Not a truth machine
when_to_use.detail: Source tags do not prove a record is correct; verify the source before operational use.

limitations.title: Missing metadata
limitations.detail: Do not fabricate a digest or locator if the packet lacks one; mark it absent.

limitations.title: Citation laundering
limitations.detail: A labeled excerpt can still mislead if it drops a qualifier; never label a paraphrase as an exact quotation or invent a bulletin end date.

limitations.title: Currentness is contextual
limitations.detail: A dated official notice may still be superseded by a newer notice outside this packet.

limitations.title: Summaries are transformations
limitations.detail: Keep the exact quote and the synthesized claim separate so a reader can inspect the change.

example.comparison_predicate: Are current hours tied to the official source, older hours labeled historical, and missing holiday hours held?
source_packet: Notice N-24, official library bulletin dated 2026-05-10, paragraph 2: "From June 1, weekday hours are 9:00–18:00 and Saturday hours are 10:00–14:00."
Blog B-19, community post dated 2024-09-05, paragraph 1: "Weekdays 9:00–17:00 and Saturdays closed."
Request: provide current regular hours and note whether holiday hours are known; no holiday notice supplied.
example.task: Draft a short reading guide for the desk; do not claim to have checked the live website.
example.baseline_instruction: Summarize the current opening hours from the packet.
example.applied_instruction: Before drafting, create a source card for EACH excerpt with ID, paragraph locator, date, exact wording, authority exactly as stated (official library bulletin or community post), digest: unavailable (no bytes or digest supplied), and any transformation into the final guide. Use the later official bulletin for the stated regular hours from June 1; label the older community post historical. For each guide sentence identify its supporting card and mark direct quote versus paraphrase versus synthesis correctly. Do not infer a bulletin end date or unchanged future hours. Holiday hours are unknown without a notice; no live verification occurred.
